Photograph: Bernat Armangué/AP View image in fullscreen Migrants in Ceuta are escorted by Spanish soldiers towards the border with Morocco on Sunday. Photograph: Bernat Armangué/AP Opinion Spain The Guardian view on events in Ceuta: chaos and tragedy are weaponised by the far right Editorial Instead of finger-pointing at Spain, mainstream EU leaders should be showing solidarity with its prime minister, Pedro Sánchez Mon 3 Aug 2026 13.30 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 14.08 EDT Share A t least 72 people are believed to have died late last week, most of them drowned or crushed as they joined tens of thousands of others in attempting to swim from Moroccan waters to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. Yet the scale of that human tragedy has barely registered, as Donald Trump has decried an “ invasion ” while European politicians exploit the crisis to serve their own agendas. If further evidence were needed of the way that the radical right increasingly distorts the terms of the migration debate in the EU, the last few days have furnished it. More needs to be understood about the drivers behind a shocking episode. Misinformation on social media – orchestrated or otherwise – appears to have played a big part, following a Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily turned back. Moroccan authorities seemingly did little to prevent the chaotic exodus, which echoed previous smaller incidents and focused international attention on a territory whose sovereignty Rabat contests. If there were online indications that such an incursion was a possibility, no alarm was sounded. The Spanish government, distracted by the need to combat ongoing wildfires, was utterly unprepared. But the vast majority of the 60,000 or so who crossed into Ceuta returned voluntarily across the border within 48 hours, some having aired grievances to reporters at the lack of work, decent wages and prospects available to them at home. The dangerous recklessness of their actions underlined the pressure-cooker levels of frustration beyond Europe’s external borders, particularly among the young. Pedro Sánchez. Photograph: Reduan Dris/EPA Subsequently, the response of leaders such as Italy’s Giorgia Meloni has been predictable but deeply dispiriting. In a performative overreaction, Ms Meloni sought to demonstrate her hard line on irregular migration by temporarily suspending Rome’s Schengen agreement with Madrid, though Ceuta has never been included in Schengen, and Italy and Spain share no border. Along with Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, she was also among 22 signatories to a letter sent to the European Commission, suggesting that the liberal migration policies of the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – which, again, have no application in Ceuta – are undermining Europe’s security. Such posturing is largely intended for a domestic audience. Mr Merz, for example, faces a major challenge from the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in three imminent state elections , while Ms Meloni is dealing with the emergence of a new party that threatens her own right flank. The zeal of such forces to weaponise the immigration issue was shown by the speed with which the AfD’s leader, Alice Weidel, claimed that the “likely destination” for most of those entering Ceuta was Germany. Hyperbolic rhetoric and finger-pointing will only undermine solidarity between European nations, and hamper attempts to deal effectively with the challenges of migration. It is impossible to cross from Ceuta into mainland Spain and the Schengen zone without passing through a checkpoint. It is also worth noting that the number of irregular border crossings into Europe in fact declined by 40% in the first half of 2026 compared with last year, partly as a result of better-coordinated preventive strategies. Instead of rounding on Mr Sánchez, mainstream European leaders should be pledging their cooperation in helping Spain to minimise the possibility of such a tragic incident ever happening again. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: The sentencing of a sex offender over the murders of Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo and Sheryl Wilkins renewed questions about how police respond to women involved in sex work. Photograph: Guy Corbishley/Alamy View image in fullscreen The sentencing of a sex offender over the murders of Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo and Sheryl Wilkins renewed questions about how police respond to women involved in sex work. Photograph: Guy Corbishley/Alamy First Edition newsletter Crime Tuesday briefing: What the Simon Levy case tells us about the women the justice system keeps failing In today’s newsletter: The women most at risk of violence are often the least likely to be heard – the murder of two sex workers shows why that must change Libby Brooks Tue 18 Aug 2026 01.42 EDT Last modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 02.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. Last week, Simon Levy, a registered sex offender, was sentenced to a rare whole life tariff for the murders of Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo and Sheryl Wilkins. Both women, as well as others targeted by Levy, were vulnerable and involved in sex work. This was no coincidence: in the sentencing remarks, it was noted that Levy – who had a history of sexual offending dating back to 2018 – selected women who sold sex as his victims because he believed he could get away with it . In the end, he couldn’t. But why did Levy – like so many sexual predators before him – assume that he could harm women involved in prostitution with impunity? Amid the diligent and necessary coverage of the police and prosecution failings that left Levy free to kill and kill again, that question was overlooked. Victims and campaigners alike have raised concerns over the way the justice system treats the experiences of such women. I’d argue that, for decades, we have been overlooking violence against sex workers. That’s the subject of today’s newsletter – but first, the headlines. Five big stories UK politics | Reform UK’s deputy leader Richard Tice dismissed efforts to tackle climate breakdown , urging British people to “enjoy” the summer heatwaves. US news | Donald Trump issued a threat to bomb Oman if the country ‘gets in the way’ of ending the US-Israel war on Iran. World news | The Ebola outbreak in DR Congo is now the deadliest in the country’s history , with at least 2,325 dead from the virus, according to official data. Jason Arday | Tens of thousands of people gathered in Trafalgar Square in London to remember and pay tribute to Jason Arday, the former Cambridge professor who died on Friday. Housing | Half of homes in Great Britain are taking longer to sell than last year as volatile conditions in the mortgage market amid the Iran war prompt buyers to “wait and see” if they can get a better deal, according to a report. In depth: The women who tell us where the danger is are being ignored View image in fullscreen Since the murders of Valencia-Trujillo and Wilkins, the Metropolitan police has sent specialist officers to Tottenham to offer support. Photograph: Sinai Noor/REX/Shutterstock A brief reflection on our media: this is the first instance I can recall in a case like this where victims were referred to as “women” first, and “sex workers” second in the majority of reporting. Coverage centred on the love in their lives, not the chaos: Carmenza’s excitement at becoming a grandmother, and Sheryl, a mother of four with “so many hopes and dreams”. And a third woman, named “ED” to protect her anonymity, who survived a brutal attack to give damning testimony: she was a classical pianist, trafficked from eastern Europe, who vowed in court “I will play music again and smile”. But here are the bald facts: women who sell sex face endemic levels of violence, and are often reluctant to report to the police because they don’t trust them to take their complaints seriously. National Ugly Mugs (NUM), a UK-wide charity working with sex workers, allows women to report violence, including anonymously, and sign up for alerts about clients to avoid. The charity says that last year, they processed 1,047 reports of varying severities of violence, but only 8% of those women consented to sharing these incidents with the police. A year before that, in 2024, a snapshot survey of women involved in prostitution across Scotland found that 90% had experienced violence, including attempted murder, while a quarter had been sexually abused as children and a sixth sexually exploited before the age of 18. That study was published around the time that Iain Packer, another serial violent offender, was jailed for 36 years for the 2005 murder of Emma Caldwell and a catalogue of sexual violence against 22 other vulnerable women working in Glasgow. The case exposed chronic police failings, finding a dismissive attitude among the police towards women selling sex, and that they had normalised the violence sex workers encountered at the hands of the men paying them. Twenty years later, policing strategy has moved on significantly – overall guidance now follows a harm reduction model, and aims to prioritise the safety of women involved. But the daily reality is that many women say this hasn’t filtered down to frontline policing and, while the focus is supposed to be on men buying sex, it’s women who are given cautions, fines, or arrested. What happened to the women who worked alongside Simon Levy’s victims? Sheryl Wilkins was murdered by Simon Levy in a Tottenham car park in August 2025, where he violently raped “ED” earlier that year. But women working alongside Wilkins had been complaining about police treatment for a year before her death, as local officers implemented ‘Clear, Hold, Build’: a national framework introduced in 2023 to tackle organised crime, which has since been used for lower-level antisocial behaviour, including begging, drug dealing and street-based sex work. ‘Closure zones’ were introduced to clear specific areas – including the same Tottenham car park – with women arrested and fined for breaching them. Police argue that the strategy was designed with safety in mind, including sign-posting women to better-lit areas. Niki Adams, of the English Collective of Prostitutes (ECP), says that women were pushed into more isolated, unlit areas. “Women try to work in pairs, so they can indicate to somebody else when they’re getting into a man’s car.” The new strategy, Adams says, broke up that arrangement. This included Sheryl Wilkins, who had been displaced from her regular spot on Fore Street. “The other women that were working with her felt outraged and upset when she was killed, because they felt that it was a direct result of this policing”. More broadly, if women feel they are on the run from the police, it affects their ability to take regular clients. By law, while exchanging sexual services for money is legal, soliciting such work is illegal. “When you’re in that situation, with pressure to earn a certain amount of money for whatever reason, you’re more likely to go with people that you otherwise would have been wary of,” says Adams . Crucially, this deprives the police of vital intelligence. “If you have a better relationship with the police, those smaller incidents get reported and a picture starts to build up if there’s a particular predator in the area,” says Adams. Since the murders of Valencia-Trujillo and Wilkins, the Met has sent specialist officers to the area with the express purpose of repairing mistrust, working alongside local charities to offer support with personal safety, housing and healthcare. Who is involved? Support agencies have been saying for some years that the group of women who sell sex is becoming increasingly diverse, as family budgets tighten during the cost of living crisis. While data is difficult to collect, estimates suggest a significant majority are mothers supporting dependent children. ECP and NUM report growing numbers of women seeking out their support services and, in a new development, some returning to prostitution having left it previously. Online adverts have changed how clients are sourced, with support groups saying the biggest threat to safety remains the fact that women risk arrest by working together indoors, pushing more of their work on to the streets. What would actually make women safer? Groups like ECP and NUM argue that decriminalising prostitution is the best way to protect women; others maintain that the focus must be on criminalising men who buy sex. It’s a debate that has polarised those who might otherwise be sisters in arms in the fight against violence against women and girls for decades. Belinda Brooks-Gordon, professor of forensic psychology at Birkbeck, has researched this territory and assessed the tides of policymaking for decades. She recalls writing to the national media with other academics in early 2006, in protest at the then Labour government’s plans to shelve managed tolerance zones in favour of a hardline approach to prostitution. “We were saying ‘this is really dangerous for women on the street’. They piloted a clampdown strategy in six cities, one of which was Ipswich. And tragically, in the autumn of that year, five women were murdered there.” Brooks-Gordon is an adviser to the National Police Chiefs’ Council’s lead on sex work and trafficking, and bears witness to a hollowing out of funding, which has affected creative pilots and even surveillance of those on the sex offender register – which Levy was on – over the decades. “You’ve got a lot of energetic, well-meaning, and highly trained people wanting to do the best they can, and the resources they’re given are thinner and thinner,” she says. She recalls the Holbeck experiment set up in Leeds in 2014 and discontinued in 2021, which allowed street sex workers to operate freely in the area without fear of arrest between the hours of 8am and 6am, but became the focus of ongoing protests by local residents for antisocial behaviour. “You have to address residents’ complaints, but where these managed zones operate they save lives – we know that from the Netherlands,” says Brooks-Gordon. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion The Merseyside model, which has now been running for 20 years, treats violence against women selling sex as a hate crime and boasted a 67% success rate for rape convictions against sex workers after its first decade. But that work has not been adopted at national level. NUM is involved with an education programme for police forces about the benefits of community liaison roles. “A lot of really good work is being done on liaison,’ says chief executive Lynsey Walton, “but even if you have the best practice in place, it’s only in recent years that sex workers have been spoken to at all, so it’s very hard to retrospectively build that trust.” But doing so, as the Levy case brings home yet again, can be a matter for life and death. “How can our criminal justice system effectively identify and stop serial perpetrators if the people they target don’t feel sufficiently safe to engage with it?” says Walton. “Prevention requires us to take seriously the people who are telling us where the danger is.” What else we’ve been enjoying View image in fullscreen Mabel Banfield-Nwachi has started writing and posting letters to her friends and family while abroad. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian Annalisa Dinnella provides an eye-opening account of the impact cuts to the Access To Work scheme is having on the arts. Sam Coare, newsletters team I’m endlessly curious about what Andy Burnham means to different demographics – here 24-year-old Ceira Sergeant argues that he signifies hope of closer ties with Europe for the generation that had no voice on Brexit. Libby As someone who has actively avoided the tennis court in this summer’s heat, Tanya Aldred, writing in this week’s Hotspot newsletter , was fascinating on how sport is adapting to our changing climate. Sam As a devoted letter-writer , especially because I live in a different city and indeed country from close friends and family, I enjoyed reading about Mabel Banfield-Nwachi’s conversion to the form. Libby As is expected of the wonderful Stevie Chick , this profile of alt-rock titan Greg Dulli is an illuminating insight into a life inside and beyond the Afghan Whigs. Sam Sport View image in fullscreen Britain’s Georgia Hunter Bell celebrates winning the women’s 1,500 meters final. Photograph: Petr David Josek/AP Athletics | Georgia Hunter Bell says she is ready to take on the ‘Big Three’ of Audrey Werro, Keely Hodgkinson and Femke Broeders-Bol in a race for the ages in Zurich next week. Fifa | The Fifa chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, has been sacked after openly criticising Gianni Infantino’s ill-fated plan to sell parts of the World Cup to private investors. Football | The Premiere League will allow audio of on-field conversations between players and referees during live broadcasts for the first time this season. The front pages View image in fullscreen Photograph: The Guardian “Tice: stop fighting climate change, enjoy heatwaves”, the Guardian’ s front page says. The Telegraph has “Rayner paves way for more traveller sites”, the Times says “Children left ‘fixated with violence’ by social media”, and the Mail leads on “So what was White house hoaxer who duped PM?”. The FT writes “KPMG and EY’s £456m deal blows hole in pledge to cut consultant costs”, the Express splashes “Smugglers use Britain as ‘transit hub’ for migrants”, and the i Paper has “Neighbours told: don’t phone 999 to report next door’s barbecue”. The Sun has “Pep’s divorce rant at players”, and Metro , on Trump’s threat to Oman, says “That doesn’t sound much like peace, Mr President”. Today in Focus View image in fullscreen Christopher Berry-Dee. Photograph: Ian Tuttle/Shutterstock A bestselling true crime author, and the crimes he’s accused of Christopher Berry-Dee has been a pioneer of the true crime genre for years. The UK’s all-time bestselling true crime author is a self-proclaimed expert in serial killers, persuading them to give interviews and laying out their crimes in extensive detail. Investigations correspondent Sirin Kale reports on the allegations of violence and sexual assault against him. Berry-Dee denies the allegations. Cartoon of the day | Nicola Jennings View image in fullscreen Illustration: Nicola Jennings/The Guardian The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad View image in fullscreen Rhossi, a critically endangered Kemp’s ridley sea turtle, is prepared to undergo a CT scan at the Houston zoo in Texas on 11 August. Photograph: Evan Garcia/Reuters When Rhossi, a young Kemp’s ridley sea turtle, was discovered on a beach in Wales in December 2023, he was fighting for his life. The Kemp’s ridley sea turtle is one of the world’s most endangered sea turtle species, and Rhossi had found himself washed up about 5,000 miles from his native Mexican and US Gulf coast region by the Atlantic Ocean’s powerful marine currents. Nearly three years on, however, Rhossi is thriving once again thanks to the intervention of Anglesey Sea zoo and, most recently, the Houston zoo, who took over Rhossi’s care after the turtle took a transatlantic flight there last week. Despite lingering pneumonia, Rhossi is reported to be “healthy, active and vigorous”, and should be fit for release back into the wild in the near future. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjej.text: Image source, Twisha's family Image caption, Twisha Sharma's death on 12 May sparked a huge media frenzy By Geeta Pandey and Vishnukant Tiwari Reporting from Delhi and Bhopal Published 3 hours ago India's federal police have filed charges in the case of a 33-year-old model and actor who was found dead in her matrimonial home in May just five months after her wedding. Twisha Sharma's death on 12 May in Bhopal city sparked a huge media frenzy, with the case making headlines every day amid rival claims of murder and suicide. In the chargesheet by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), Twisha's husband and mother-in-law have been charged with "abetment to suicide" and "cruelty". Her husband Samarth Singh, a lawyer, and mother-in-law Giribala Singh, a retired judge, have denied the allegations against them. Warning: This article contains details some readers may find distressing. Image source, Photo credit Twisha's family Image caption, Twisha and Samarth had been married only for five months Twisha's death has generated an extraordinary interest in India because in public perception, members of India's powerful judiciary are meant to lead by example. Twisha's parents and siblings alleged that she was tortured by Singh and his mother over dowry demands and that she was murdered. Giribala called the accusations "baseless" and alleged that Twisha had mental health issues and that she killed herself. Samarth initially could not be located but later surrendered to police. Giribala was arrested a few days later and the mother and son remain in jail. "Due to continuous mental cruelty at the hands of both the accused [Twisha's husband and mother-in-law], she was left with no option but to end her life," the CBI said in the 600-page chargesheet submitted in the court last week. Twisha's family lawyer Ankur Pandey told BBC Hindi that since the CBI has invoked sections related to abetment to suicide, "it means that the investigation has considered the death to be an alleged suicide". He said the CBI has sought permission from the court for further investigation, saying that "if new evidence emerges during the investigation, role of some more people can be investigated and, if needed, a supplementary chargesheet can be filed". Giribala Singh's lawyer Inosh George Carlo told the BBC, "The investigation has found no evidence of the earlier allegations of dowry harassment and murder... We have been saying this from the beginning but the media never listened to us." Image source, ANI Image caption, Retired judge Giribala Singh (right) has been criticised for discussing Twisha's health issues in public A model and actor, Twisha was crowned Miss Pune in 2012 after winning a beauty pageant in the western Indian city. She had featured in a number of advertising campaigns and acted in a Telugu-language film. In recent years, she had also worked as a marketing professional with private firms. According to the chargesheet, Twisha met Samarth through a dating app in February 2025 and the couple married in December. In the chargesheet, the CBI said its investigation showed that after their marriage, Samarth subjected Twisha to mental cruelty on several occasions and repeatedly used derogatory terms towards her. "Giribala Singh would from time to time instigate her son to commit mental cruelty on Twisha," it added. According to Twisha's parental family, the biggest point of friction between her and her in-laws came in April after she became pregnant. They allege that "her husband and mother-in-law questioned her character and accused her of carrying someone else's baby" and "forced her to undergo an abortion in the first week of May". Giribala Singh had denied the allegations, saying it was Twisha who insisted on the abortion saying that she did not want children. Days after Twisha's death, the former judge had drawn criticism for addressing a press conference and giving media interviews where she discussed her daughter-in-law's mental health and called her "liberal" - when asked to explain the term by an interviewer, she spoke of "promiscuity". Her comments led to a huge outrage and Twisha's father said it was an attempt to tarnish his daughter's name.
